C0.quote: We model the problem as an approval-based multiwinner election
C0.note: Agents' approvals are aggregated by multiwinner voting rules into a committee of matchings.

C1.quote: we analyze the computational complexity of computing winning committees
C1.note: Sections 3.2 and 4 hold most results (algorithms, NP-hardness). Section 5 holds the axiomatic results (EJR, core).

C2.1.value: preference profile; approval set; approval preferences
C2.1.quote: A = (Aa )a∈N a preference profile with Aa ⊆ N \ {a}

C2.2.quote: based on the agents’ dichotomous (i.e., approval/disapproval) preferences over each other
C2.2.note: Approval sets over agents, lifted to approvals over matchings.

C2.3.quote: approval sets of students could, for example, consist of all students they like
C2.3.note: The held attitude is the agents' preferences or liking. These are not defined separately from the input; the input itself is called preferences.

C2.4.quote: A = (Aa )a∈N a preference profile with Aa ⊆ C
C2.4.note: The rule is applied directly to the preference profile, with no statement about reporting or submission.

C3.1.note: No manipulation or strategic reporting is analysed.

C4.1.quote: we let the happiness score ha (W ) of a denote the number
C4.1.note: Satisfaction is defined as the number of approved candidates in the committee.

C4.2.quote: number of (copies of) candidates from W approved by a
C4.2.note: Doubt: the happiness score implies utility 1 per approved matching, but the paper never states what the two classes mean in utility terms. Y was chosen as the first-listed code.

C5.1.quote: Seq-w-Thiele satisfies EJR in all symmetric matching elections.
C5.1.note: Results use proportional representation axioms (PJR, EJR, core stability) and Pareto optimal matchings.

C5.2.note: Axioms are evaluated on approval sets, with no statement relating them to held attitudes.

VOT.note: Approval sets are exogenous inputs to the rule.
